description: Five short synthetic research papers written for ResearchMate's evaluation. The methods, authors and results are fictional; dataset names are used only as realistic vocabulary. Two papers share a topic (federated learning) so that retrieval has to tell similar papers apart.

papers.title: ProxAvg: Proximal Local Objectives for Federated Optimization on Heterogeneous Devices
papers.authors: Mira Okafor, Daniel Reyes, Hana Lindqvist
pages:
Abstract
Federated learning trains a shared model across many devices without moving their raw data to a server. In practice the devices differ in hardware and in the data they hold, and the standard averaging approach becomes unstable when local datasets are not identically distributed. We introduce ProxAvg, which adds a proximal penalty to every local objective so that local models cannot drift far from the current global model. ProxAvg also accepts partial work, letting slow devices return fewer local steps instead of being dropped. Across four benchmarks, ProxAvg converges more reliably than plain averaging and improves final test accuracy by up to 18 percentage points in the most heterogeneous settings.
1 Introduction
In federated learning a server repeatedly sends the global model to a sample of devices, each device trains on its own data, and the server averages the returned models. This loop works well when every device holds a similar slice of the data. Real deployments rarely look like that: phones collect different kinds of text and images, and their processors, batteries and network links vary widely. Two problems follow. Statistical heterogeneity means that local optima pull in different directions, so averaging them can move the global model away from a good solution. Systems heterogeneity means that some devices cannot finish the requested amount of work before the round ends, and discarding them biases training toward fast devices.

2 Method
ProxAvg keeps the communication pattern of federated averaging but changes what each device optimises. Instead of minimising its local loss alone, device k minimises the local loss plus a penalty equal to mu divided by two times the squared distance between its weights and the global weights received at the start of the round. The coefficient mu controls how strongly local updates are tied to the global model: with mu equal to zero ProxAvg reduces to plain averaging, and larger values make local models more conservative. Because the penalty is added to the objective, any local solver can be used, and devices may run a different number of steps. We call the amount of local progress a device achieves its gamma-inexact solution, and the server accepts whatever a device returns by the deadline rather than discarding stragglers.
We analyse ProxAvg under a bounded dissimilarity assumption, which limits how different the gradients of local objectives can be from the global gradient. Under this assumption, and for a suitable choice of mu, the expected decrease of the global objective per round is positive even when devices perform very different amounts of work.

3 Experimental Setup
We evaluate on four federated benchmarks. MNIST and FEMNIST are image classification tasks partitioned so that each device sees only a few classes. Shakespeare is a next-character prediction task in which each speaking role is a device. Sent140 is a sentiment classification task over tweets grouped by user. We use a multinomial logistic regression model for MNIST and FEMNIST and a two-layer LSTM for Shakespeare and Sent140. In every round the server samples ten devices, each device runs up to twenty local epochs, and we simulate systems heterogeneity by giving a random 90 percent of devices a smaller amount of work. The proximal coefficient mu is chosen from 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 and 1 on a validation split; mu equal to 0.01 worked best on Shakespeare and mu equal to 1 on MNIST. All experiments run on a single machine that simulates the devices sequentially.
4 Results
With 90 percent stragglers, plain averaging that drops slow devices diverges on two of the four tasks, while ProxAvg converges on all of them. On the most heterogeneous partitions ProxAvg improves absolute test accuracy by 18 percentage points on average over plain averaging. Even without stragglers, a small positive mu reduces the variance of the training loss between rounds.

5 Limitations
Our convergence analysis relies on the bounded dissimilarity assumption, which may not hold for adversarial or extremely skewed federations. The best value of mu differs across datasets and must be tuned, and we do not provide a rule for setting it without validation data. All devices are simulated on one machine, so we do not measure wall-clock time, energy use or real network delays.
6 Future Work
We plan to choose mu adaptively during training from the observed dissimilarity between local updates. Another direction is to combine the proximal penalty with privacy mechanisms such as secure aggregation and to evaluate ProxAvg on real devices with intermittent connectivity.

papers.title: DriftGuard: Correcting Client Drift in Federated Learning with Control Variates
papers.authors: Tomas Varga, Priya Raman, Elena Costa
pages:
Abstract
When clients in federated learning hold different data distributions, their local updates drift toward their own optima, which slows convergence of federated averaging. We present DriftGuard, an algorithm that estimates the update direction of the server and of each client and uses the difference as a control variate to correct every local step. DriftGuard needs significantly fewer communication rounds than federated averaging to reach a target accuracy, and its convergence does not degrade as client heterogeneity grows. The price is that each round transmits a correction vector in addition to the model, which doubles the upload size.
1 Introduction
Federated averaging performs several local steps on each client before the server averages the results. Local steps save communication, but on heterogeneous data each client moves toward the minimiser of its own loss. We call this effect client drift. The more local steps a client takes, the further it drifts, so practitioners face a trade-off between communication cost and the quality of the averaged model. Existing remedies such as decaying the learning rate or reducing the number of local steps remove much of the benefit of local training. DriftGuard instead keeps many local steps and removes the drift itself.

2 Method
DriftGuard maintains a server control variate c and a client control variate c_i for every participating client. Each variate estimates the gradient direction of the corresponding objective. During local training, client i corrects every stochastic gradient by subtracting c_i and adding c, so that its update follows the global direction rather than its local one. After training, the client refreshes c_i from the change in its model and sends both the model delta and the change in its control variate to the server. The server averages both quantities, which keeps c an unbiased estimate of the average client direction. When all clients share the same data distribution the correction is zero in expectation and DriftGuard behaves like federated averaging.
We prove that for strongly convex objectives DriftGuard converges at a rate that does not depend on the dissimilarity between clients, and that it tolerates sampling only a small fraction of clients in each round.

3 Experimental Setup
We evaluate DriftGuard on the extended MNIST dataset EMNIST with 400 simulated clients, where each client mostly holds a single character class, and on CIFAR-10 split across 100 clients with a Dirichlet concentration of 0.1. Every round samples 20 percent of the clients. Clients use a learning rate of 0.05 and five local epochs with a batch size of 50. The baselines are federated averaging, federated averaging with a decaying learning rate, and a proximal method with mu equal to 0.1. We report the number of communication rounds needed to reach 0.5 test accuracy on EMNIST and 70 percent test accuracy on CIFAR-10.
4 Results
On EMNIST, DriftGuard reaches 0.5 test accuracy in 31 rounds, compared with 148 rounds for federated averaging and 92 rounds for the proximal baseline. On CIFAR-10 it reaches 70 percent accuracy in 210 rounds while federated averaging needs 590. The advantage grows with the number of local epochs, which confirms that the correction removes drift rather than simply slowing local training.

5 Limitations
DriftGuard doubles the upload per round because each client sends its control variate update together with the model update. Clients must also store their control variate between rounds, which is a problem for clients that participate only once or rarely, since their stored variate becomes stale. Our theory assumes full gradients for the variance analysis and strongly convex losses for the main rate.
6 Future Work
Compressing the control variate updates could remove most of the extra communication. We also want to study stateless variants for cross-device settings in which most clients are seen only once.

papers.title: FuseRank: Combining Lexical and Dense Retrieval for Grounded Question Answering
papers.authors: Samuel Adeyemi, Lucia Ferrante, Kenji Watanabe
pages:
Abstract
Question answering systems that ground their answers in a document collection depend on retrieving the right passages. Dense retrievers match paraphrases but miss rare identifiers, while lexical retrievers such as BM25 match exact terms but fail when the question uses different words from the document. FuseRank merges the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion and then rescores the top candidates with a cross-encoder. On a benchmark of technical documentation questions, FuseRank raises recall at 10 from 0.71 for dense retrieval alone to 0.86, and answers generated from its passages contain fewer unsupported claims.
1 Introduction
Retrieval-augmented generation answers a question by first retrieving passages and then asking a language model to answer from them. When the retriever misses the passage that contains the answer, the model either refuses or, worse, answers from its own memory. Embedding models map questions and passages into a shared vector space, which captures meaning but blurs exact strings such as error codes, version numbers and product names. Keyword retrieval has the opposite profile. Engineers often pick one method and accept its blind spots. We argue that the two are complementary and that combining them is cheap.

2 Method
FuseRank runs a dense retriever and BM25 independently over the same passages. The dense retriever encodes passages with a sentence embedding model and searches them with exact inner-product search. BM25 scores passages by term frequency with saturation and document length normalisation. Because the two scores are on different scales, FuseRank does not combine scores; it uses reciprocal rank fusion, which gives each passage the sum of one divided by k plus its rank in each list, with k equal to 60. The top 20 fused candidates are then scored by a cross-encoder that reads the question and each passage together, and the best eight passages are passed to the generator. The generator must cite passage identifiers for every claim, and answers whose citations do not match a retrieved passage are rejected.

3 Experimental Setup
We built TechDocQA, a benchmark of 1,200 questions over 40,000 passages from open-source software documentation, where each question is labelled with the passages that answer it. About a third of the questions mention an exact identifier such as a configuration key or an error code. We compare dense retrieval, BM25, fusion without reranking and full FuseRank, and report recall at 10 and mean reciprocal rank. Answers are produced by the same instruction-tuned model for every configuration, and two annotators judged whether each claim was supported by the cited passages.
4 Results
Dense retrieval reaches a recall at 10 of 0.71 and BM25 reaches 0.64, but on questions with exact identifiers BM25 is better by 19 points. Fusion alone raises recall at 10 to 0.82, and reranking with the cross-encoder raises it to 0.86 and mean reciprocal rank from 0.58 to 0.69. Unsupported claims in generated answers fall from 14 percent with dense retrieval to 6 percent with FuseRank.

5 Limitations
The cross-encoder adds about 120 milliseconds of latency per question on a CPU, which may be too slow for interactive use on large candidate sets. TechDocQA contains only English software documentation, so the gains may differ for other domains and languages. Our claim annotations come from two annotators and cover a sample of 300 answers rather than the full benchmark.
6 Future Work
We plan to learn the fusion weights per query type instead of using a fixed constant, and to test whether a small reranker distilled from the cross-encoder keeps most of the gain at lower latency.

papers.title: LayerAlign: Compact Student Models through Layer-Aligned Knowledge Distillation
papers.authors: Aisha Bello, Marcus Holm, Yuki Tanaka
pages:
Abstract
Large pretrained language models are expensive to serve. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher, but students usually copy only the output distribution of the teacher. LayerAlign also aligns intermediate representations: each student layer is mapped to a teacher layer and trained to reproduce its hidden states and attention patterns. A six-layer student distilled with LayerAlign retains 97 percent of the average score of its twelve-layer teacher on the GLUE benchmark while running 2.1 times faster.
1 Introduction
Distillation compresses a model by transferring knowledge from a teacher to a student with fewer parameters. The classic objective matches softened output probabilities, which carries information about how the teacher ranks wrong answers. Intermediate layers carry richer signals, but students and teachers have different depths, so it is unclear which layers should be matched. Prior choices are ad hoc, such as matching every second teacher layer. We propose a principled mapping and show that it matters more than the exact loss used for alignment.

2 Method
LayerAlign first measures how similar each teacher layer is to each student layer at initialisation using centred kernel alignment on a small batch of unlabelled text. It then solves a monotone assignment problem so that lower student layers map to lower teacher layers and the total similarity is maximised. Training combines three losses: the cross-entropy between softened teacher and student outputs with a temperature of 4, a mean squared error between projected student hidden states and their assigned teacher hidden states, and a Kullback-Leibler loss between attention distributions. A learned linear projection handles the different hidden sizes. The three losses are weighted equally, which we found robust across tasks.

3 Experimental Setup
The teacher is a twelve-layer transformer encoder with 110 million parameters. Students have six layers and a hidden size of 768, or four layers and a hidden size of 312. We distil on general English text for three epochs and then fine-tune on each task of the GLUE benchmark, which includes sentiment, paraphrase and natural language inference tasks. Inference speed is measured on a single CPU core with a batch size of one and a sequence length of 128 tokens. We compare against output-only distillation and against students that match every second teacher layer.
4 Results
The six-layer student keeps 97 percent of the average GLUE score of the teacher and is 2.1 times faster; the four-layer student keeps 92 percent and is 7.4 times faster. Matching every second layer keeps 95 percent for the six-layer student, so the learned mapping adds two points. Removing the attention loss costs one point on average, and removing the hidden-state loss costs three.

5 Limitations
LayerAlign requires access to the internal states of the teacher, so it cannot distil from models that are only available through an API. Computing the layer mapping adds a preprocessing step, and the mapping is fixed after initialisation even though layer roles may change during training. We evaluate only English encoder models; generative decoder models and multilingual settings are untested.
6 Future Work
A natural extension is to update the layer mapping during training. We also want to apply LayerAlign to decoder-only models used for text generation.

papers.title: SolvGAT: Graph Attention Networks for Predicting Aqueous Solubility of Small Molecules
papers.authors: Ingrid Sorensen, Kofi Mensah, Ravi Iyer
pages:
Abstract
Aqueous solubility determines whether a drug candidate can be absorbed, yet measuring it is slow and costly. We present SolvGAT, a graph attention network that treats a molecule as a graph of atoms and bonds and learns which neighbouring atoms matter for solubility. On the ESOL dataset SolvGAT reaches a root mean squared error of 0.52 log units, improving on fingerprint-based random forests and on graph convolutional networks. Attention weights highlight polar functional groups that chemists associate with higher solubility.
1 Introduction
Early-stage drug discovery screens thousands of candidate molecules, and poorly soluble compounds often fail later in development. Computational predictors let chemists discard such candidates early. Classical approaches compute fixed molecular fingerprints and train a regression model on them. Graph neural networks instead learn representations directly from the molecular graph, where atoms are nodes and bonds are edges. Most graph models weight all neighbours of an atom equally, although some substructures, such as hydroxyl groups, influence solubility much more than others.

2 Method
SolvGAT represents each atom by its element, degree, formal charge, hybridisation and aromaticity, and each bond by its type and whether it is in a ring. Four graph attention layers update atom features by attending over neighbouring atoms, with eight attention heads per layer and edge features added to the attention scores. A gated readout sums atom features into a single molecule vector, which a two-layer perceptron maps to a solubility value in log moles per litre. We train with mean squared error and use dropout of 0.2 between attention layers.

3 Experimental Setup
We use the ESOL dataset of 1,128 molecules with measured aqueous solubility and a scaffold split, which places structurally different molecules in the training and test sets, with 80 percent for training, 10 percent for validation and 10 percent for testing. Baselines are a random forest on extended-connectivity fingerprints with radius 2, a graph convolutional network and a message passing neural network. Each model is trained five times with different random seeds and we report the mean root mean squared error. Training takes about four minutes per run on one consumer GPU.
4 Results
SolvGAT reaches a root mean squared error of 0.52 log units on the scaffold test split, compared with 0.58 for the message passing network, 0.61 for the graph convolutional network and 0.99 for the random forest. Visualising attention shows that hydroxyl, amine and carboxyl groups receive the highest weights, consistent with their known effect on solubility.

5 Limitations
ESOL is small, so differences between neural models are within two standard deviations on some seeds. Measured solubility values contain experimental noise of roughly half a log unit, which bounds the achievable error. SolvGAT ignores three-dimensional conformation and temperature, both of which affect solubility.
6 Future Work
We plan to pretrain the attention layers on large unlabelled molecule collections and to add three-dimensional coordinates. Extending the model to predict solubility in organic solvents is another direction.
